Following is a summary of the HUD requirements for noise levels occurring for eight hours in a 24-hour period:

Standards for interior noise exposure state that for sleeping quarters noise levels should not exceed 45 dBA for more than 8 hours in a 24-hour period. The consultant study used this 45 dBA requirement for all interior spaces of residential units.
(4) Methodology: Noise level contours were established on an Illustrative Site Plan for the completed Randolph Project in order to graphically demonstrate the effect of acoustic shielding that will be provided by existing and proposed buildings on site. All buildings were computed as two-story structures ranging between 20 and 25 feet in height. In turn, all noise levels were calculated for a height of 15 feet above ground level, the approximate height of second story windows. This height is considered the uppermost level that noise would be able to penetrate into interior living spaces through an exterior wall component of relatively low acoustical shielding value (glass). Second floor apartments are generally exposed to higher noise levels than the first floor units or eye-level heights outdoors, and therefore, the expected second floor level should determine adherance to the given criteria.
Exhibit No. 6 in the Appendix gives a graphical representation of the external noise exposure standards. The approximate location of 65 dBA contours divides the site into two categories, Normally Acceptable and Normally Unacceptable. The Normally Unacceptable portion is indicated by shading. In addition, residential buildings which are exposed to noise levels between 70 and 75 dBA have been blacked in as those most impacted by airborne noise.
